chapter_seo_title: Dao Gui Yi Xian Ch. 388 – Li Huowang’s Apology to Yang Na
chapter_meta_description: Li Huowang escapes one monster only to face the one he can't fight: Yang Na's love. A heart-wrenching chapter of madness, masks, and a tiny white flower.
og_title: "I'm Sorry..."—The Most Devastating Line in Dao Gui Yi Xian Chapter 388
og_description: In a prison yard, Li Huowang chooses madness over facing Yang Na's pain. An apology whispered through blood.
twitter_title: Li Huowang’s fake Sun Wukong act breaks our hearts
twitter_description: He escaped the belly of a monster, but he couldn't escape her eyes. Chapter 388 is pure emotional devastation.

lore_anchors.definition: The central hero of *Journey to the West*, a mythical monkey with immense power who once rebelled against the heavens. Li Huowang claims this identity to mask his own vulnerability.
The modern-world counterpart to the White Jade Capital in the novel’s meta-structure, appearing as a psychiatric detention facility.
A high-voltage barrier used in prison security; Li Huowang’s ability to climb through it despite severe burns demonstrates his inhuman pain tolerance.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Why does Li Huowang pretend to be Sun Wukong?
cultural_notes_faq.a: He uses the mad performance as a shield to keep Yang Na from truly seeing the broken man he’s become, so she will finally give up on him and save herself from more pain.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Is Li Huowang actually in the water?
cultural_notes_faq.a: No, he is in a prison exercise yard. His perception is warped by hallucination and trauma, interpreting the watchtower as a boat and the guards as water monsters.

cultural_notes_faq.q: What does the tiny wildflower symbolize?
cultural_notes_faq.a: It represents the last uncorrupted, gentle part of Li Huowang’s soul—fragile, small, and offered as a silent goodbye and apology.
